title: The Life and Intellectual Legacy of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui: A Synthesis of Science, Rabbinics, and Rationalism in 17th-Century Tlemcen
source_file: The Life and Intellectual Legacy of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui_ A Synthesis of Science, Rabbinics, and Rationalism in 17th-Century Tlemcen.docx
content:
The seventeenth century in the Maghreb represented a period of profound cultural transition, where the remnants of the Sephardic Golden Age integrated with the local traditions of North African Jewry under the umbrella of Ottoman governance. At the epicenter of this intellectual fusion stood Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui (1603–1704), a figure whose life and work provide a comprehensive window into the "Jerusalem of the West"—the Jewish community of Tlemcen, Algeria.[1, 2] Rabbi Saadia was not merely a local communal leader; he was a polymath who bridged the gap between the rigorous demands of rabbinic law and the systematic beauty of the mathematical sciences. His work, Mone Mispar, stands as a landmark in the history of Jewish education in the Maghreb, representing one of the earliest instances of a formal mathematics treatise written in Hebrew for the specific purpose of religious and communal instruction.[2] Furthermore, his staunch opposition to the Sabbatean movement during its peak in the mid-seventeenth century underscores a commitment to a rationalist, traditionalist framework that defined the Algerian rabbinate for generations.[1]
Historical Foundations of Tlemcen Jewry: The Jerusalem of the West
To understand the scope of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui’s work, the socio-cultural environment of Tlemcen must be analyzed in its historical depth. Tlemcen earned its moniker as the "Jerusalem of the West" not merely for its piety but for its role as a sanctuary for Jewish scholarship following the successive upheavals of the Iberian Peninsula.[2] The community’s character was fundamentally transformed by the arrival of Spanish refugees (Megorashim) following the persecutions of 1391 and the final expulsion in 1492.[2, 3] These exiles brought with them the high Sephardic culture, characterized by a unique integration of Torah study with philosophy, medicine, and the sciences.
The most influential figure of this transition was Rabbi Ephraim Encaoua (Anqāwa), a physician and theologian from Toledo who arrived in Tlemcen in 1391.[2, 3] Encaoua’s legacy established the community as a bastion of Sephardic rationalism. He is credited with obtaining the right for Jews to live inside the city walls; previously, they were relegated to Agardir.[2] By the time Saadia Chouraqui was born in 1603, the community had successfully integrated the Megorashim (exiled) and the Toshavim (autochthonous Jews), with the Spanish influence remaining dominant in liturgy and rabbinic methodology.[2] This dual heritage provided the fertile soil in which Chouraqui’s polymathic interests could grow.
The socio-political dynamics of the seventeenth century, during which Rabbi Saadia lived nearly in its entirety, were characterized by relative stability under Ottoman rule, punctuated by moments of local volatility. The Jewish community enjoyed a degree of autonomy, yet they were subject to the whims of local governors and the broader Mediterranean geopolitical struggle. For instance, in 1517, Ottoman pirate raids had led to the loss of Jewish property and the imposition of restrictive clothing.[2] However, by the 1600s, the community had established a robust internal structure. This environment necessitated leaders who could defend the community not only from external threats but also from internal theological fissures. Rabbi Saadia’s education, which combined traditional Talmudic mastery with philosophy and mathematics, was a direct response to the need for a well-rounded, rational leadership that could navigate these complexities.[1]
The Mathematical Contribution: Mone Mispar
The most distinct element of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui’s legacy is his contribution to the mathematical sciences. In an era where secular studies were often viewed with suspicion in many parts of the Jewish world, the Maghrebi tradition—inherited from the Spanish Golden Age—maintained that mathematics was an essential tool for the religious scholar.[2, 4] His treatise, Mone Mispar (The Calculator of Numbers), written in Hebrew, was designed as a pedagogical tool for Jewish students in Tlemcen.[2]
Structure and Pedagogical Purpose
The title Mone Mispar is evocative of the biblical scribe or the "counter" of Israel, yet its content was rigorously technical and practical. The work was not merely a theoretical exploration of number theory; it was a manual intended to equip students with the arithmetic skills necessary for both commercial life and the complex calculations required by Jewish law.[2] In the 17th-century Maghreb, Jewish communal life required sophisticated mathematical applications in several areas:
Estate Division: Calculating inheritance according to the complex ratios prescribed in the Talmud.
Calendar Calculations: Determining the Molad (lunar birth) and the intercalation of leap years.
Commerce: Managing the arithmetic of trade in a Mediterranean hub where Jews often served as intermediaries.[2]
The impact of this work was significant enough to warrant a modern critical edition by Gad B. Sarfatti in 1973.[4] Sarfatti’s analysis highlights that while Chouraqui was not a "professional mathematician" in the modern sense, his work shows how elementary arithmetic had become an established, integrated component of even a purely religious education in the North African context.[4] The use of Hebrew for these concepts was a deliberate choice to ensure that the "wisdom of the nations" remained accessible within the framework of holy study, reinforcing the Maimonidean idea that understanding the physical world is a precursor to understanding the Creator.[1]
Mathematical Methodology and Content
Mone Mispar covers various aspects of arithmetic, including operations with integers and fractions. Chouraqui’s approach reflects the seepage of scientific knowledge from professional circles to the educated laity.[4] For example, the text explores the division and ratio of fractions, such as:

The treatise also addresses more complex ratios and the "Rule of Three," which was essential for mercantile calculations.[4] The technicality of the work suggests that the "educated laity" of Tlemcen possessed a high degree of quantitative literacy.
The Struggle Against Sabbateanism
Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui’s career coincided with one of the most tumultuous episodes in Jewish history: the rise of Sabbatai Zevi. In 1666, Zevi’s claim to be the Messiah swept through the Jewish world, creating a crisis of authority and belief. The movement was characterized by mystical fervor, the abandonment of traditional fast days, and a radical departure from established rabbinic norms.
Rationalist Opposition to Messianic Fervor
Chouraqui’s opposition to the Sabbatean movement was not merely a matter of communal policy; it was deeply rooted in his philosophical and mathematical training.[1] As a follower of the rationalist tradition, he viewed the messianic hysteria as a violation of the logical and legal structures of Judaism. While many communities in North Africa were initially swept up in the excitement, Chouraqui remained a bulwark of skepticism.[1]
His struggle against the movement can be understood through three distinct lenses:
Legal Rationalism: Chouraqui demanded empirical and legal proof for any claim of messianic status. The mystical justifications provided by Zevi’s followers—often involving Gematria (numerical values) and Kabbalistic visions—were viewed by Chouraqui as insufficient and dangerous deviations from normative Halakha.[1]
Communal Stability: Tlemcen’s status as a stable religious center (the "Jerusalem of the West") was at risk if the community succumbed to the antinomian tendencies of the Zevists, which included the suspension of certain religious prohibitions.
Intellectual Pedigree: As a scholar who lived to the age of 101, Chouraqui represented a direct link to the pre-Sabbatean traditions of Tlemcen.[1] His longevity allowed him to witness the rise, peak, and eventual collapse of the movement, providing him with a long-term perspective that younger, more excitable leaders lacked.
The fact that Chouraqui is remembered specifically for this struggle indicates that his role was pivotal in ensuring that the Tlemcen community remained anchored in traditional practice.[1] His rationalist approach filtered the messianic claims through the lens of established rabbinic wisdom, effectively inoculating a significant portion of the community against the radicalism of the era.
Liturgical and Poetic Contributions
Beyond his roles as a mathematician and communal defender, Rabbi Saadia was a gifted poet and liturgist. The creation of Piyyutim (liturgical poems) was a hallmark of the rabbis of Tlemcen, who often incorporated these works into the distinct Tlemcen rite.[2]
Characteristics of the Tlemcen Piyyut
The Jewish community of Tlemcen maintained a repertoire of poems that were chanted during religious services, often reflecting the unique history and hardships of the community.[2] Chouraqui’s contributions to this genre are noted for their linguistic precision and philosophical depth.[1] The Tlemcen liturgical tradition, influenced by the Sephardic school, utilized strict meter and rhyme, often embedding philosophical or mathematical truths within the devotional text.
The lists of Piyyutim associated with the North African and broader Jewish tradition highlight themes of divine praise, national longing, and the search for wisdom.[5, 6] In the specific context of Tlemcen, these poems served as a "communal memory," preserving the Hebrew language and Sephardic poetic meters in an environment where Arabic was the daily tongue.[2]
Philosophy and Torah Outlook: The Meshnatoh HaToranit
The "Torah Path" (Meshnatoh HaToranit) of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui was one of deliberate synthesis. He did not see a contradiction between the study of Euclid and the study of the Talmud. Rather, he viewed them as complementary facets of a single, unified truth.[1]
The Influence of the Spanish Rationalists
As a scholar in the Maghreb, Chouraqui was a spiritual heir to the works of Maimonides and Ibn Ezra. This tradition held that science is a "handmaid to theology"—one cannot fully grasp the intricacies of the law, such as the measurements of the Tabernacle or the timing of the holidays, without a firm grounding in geometry and astronomy. Reason served as a filter; mystical experiences had to be measured against the standard of human reason and the received law. This explains his rigorous rejection of the Sabbatean movement.[1]
His long life (1603–1704) allowed him to mentor several generations of students, instilling in them this balanced approach.[1] This intellectual lineage would eventually reach into the modern era, influencing descendants and later scholars who sought to reconcile Jewish identity with the broader world of knowledge.
The Physical and Spiritual Center: The Synagogue de la Rue Marmol
The physical embodiment of the Tlemcen community's spirit was found in its synagogues. While Rabbi Saadia would have prayed in the older quarters of the city, the legacy of his community was preserved in structures like the Synagogue de la Rue Marmol.[2] Built between 1830 and 1940, this synagogue served as a bridge between the medieval history of Tlemcen and the modern era.
During times of anti-Semitic discrimination, particularly under the Vichy regime in the 1940s, the synagogue functioned as more than a house of prayer; it became a private secondary school for Jewish students who were barred from public education.[2] This continues the pedagogical tradition established by Chouraqui—using communal spaces to provide a holistic education, including both religious and secular subjects. The synagogue's eventual collapse in 1941 marked a symbolic end to an era of Jewish presence that had lasted for a millennium.[2]
The Chouraqui Lineage and Modern Legacy
The name Chouraqui (or Shoraki) remained prominent in Algerian Jewish history long after Saadia’s death. The continuity of the family’s intellectual engagement—from the seventeenth-century rabbi writing math treatises in Hebrew to modern philosophers—highlights a persistent theme in Tlemcen Jewry: the commitment to universal knowledge within a deeply Jewish framework.[2, 7]
One of the most notable modern figures in this lineage is André Chouraqui (1917–2007), a renowned translator of the Bible and communal leader.[7] André Chouraqui’s education mirrored the polymathic nature of his ancestor; he studied law in Paris while simultaneously pursuing Hebrew and Aramaic studies at the Ecole Rabbinique de France.[7] His life, spanning the resistance during World War II and a prominent career in Israel, represents the ripple effects of the Tlemcen intellectual tradition in the 20th century.
Conclusion: The Centenarian of Reason
Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui’s life spans the distance between the post-Renaissance era and the dawn of the Enlightenment. In the specific context of the Ottoman Maghreb, he represented the peak of Sephardic rabbinic culture. By authoring Mone Mispar, he democratized mathematical knowledge for the Jewish youth of Tlemcen, ensuring that their religious education was grounded in the realities of the physical world.[2, 4] By standing against the Sabbatean movement, he preserved the legal and rational integrity of his community during a time of global Jewish crisis.[1]
His legacy is one of synthesis: a scholar who was as comfortable with the "count of numbers" as he was with the "count of the commandments." For the "Jerusalem of the West," Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui was not just a leader, but a living bridge between the lost glory of Spain and the enduring resilience of the North African tradition. His work ensures that the intellectual history of Tlemcen is remembered not only for its piety but for its commitment to the universal language of mathematics and the rational pursuit of truth.

title: The Work, Torah Teaching and Legacy of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui of the Sages of Tlemcen: A Comprehensive Study of His Life, Writings, Halakhic Rulings and the Chouraqui Family

The Work, Torah Teaching and Legacy of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui of the Sages of Tlemcen: A Comprehensive Study of His Life, Writings, Halakhic Rulings and the Chouraqui Family
Introduction and Historical Context: The Jewish Community of Tlemcen in the 17th Century
The city of Tlemcen, located in the western region of Algeria near the Moroccan border, served for hundreds of years as one of the most prominent spiritual, cultural and halakhic centers in the Maghreb [cite: 1, 2]. Since the waves of immigration of the exiles from Spain at the end of the 14th century and in the 15th century, led by early sages such as Rabbi Ephraim Ankawa, the Jewish community of the city was marked by a unique synthesis between the Spanish-Andalusian Talmudic tradition and scientific inquiry and local spiritual creativity [cite: 1, 2]. In the 17th and 18th centuries, under the rule of the Ottoman Empire, the community experienced a scholarly flowering expressed in a renewal of Talmudic and halakhic study, with a profound integration of biblical exegesis, Kabbalah, the Hebrew language, philosophy and the natural sciences [cite: 1, 3].
At the center of this flowering stood the figure of Rabbi Saadia ben Eliyahu Chouraqui, one of the greatest sages and liturgical poets of Tlemcen, who was active over a full century and left an indelible mark on the intellectual legacy of North African Jewry in the early modern period [cite: 1]. The figure of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui represents the classic type of the multidisciplinary sage of the Mediterranean world, who saw general wisdom and the sciences of his time as complementary tools for understanding the Torah of Israel and for leading the public [cite: 1]. His spiritual work interwove the composition of works in the exact sciences, hermeneutical biblical exegesis, extensive liturgical creativity and a determined ideological struggle against the Sabbatean movement, which endangered the cohesion of the communities in the region [cite: 1].
His Life, Intellectual Portrait and Place in the Spiritual Leadership
Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui was born in Tlemcen in 1603 (5363) to his father, Rabbi Eliyahu Chouraqui, a member of a distinguished rabbinic family of exiles from Spain that settled in North Africa after the expulsion of 5252 [cite: 1, 4]. Rabbi Saadia was blessed with exceptional longevity, living over a hundred years, and died in 1704 (5464), leaving behind an extensive written oeuvre and generations of students [cite: 1, 5]. The environment in which he grew up in Tlemcen brought together the rabbinic teachings of the exiles from Spain and the culture of the sages of the Maghreb, which shaped his comprehensive education, including full mastery of Talmud, halakha, Hebrew linguistics and Kabbalah, alongside expertise in mathematics, astronomy and natural philosophy [cite: 1].
His standing in Torah and science earned deep esteem among the sages of his generation throughout North Africa [cite: 1]. The spiritual leader of Moroccan Jewry, Rabbi Yaakov Ibn Tzur (the Yaavetz of Fez), lavished praise on Rabbi Saadia and wrote of him that "in every wisdom his right hand is exalted," an expression reflecting the recognition by the sages of the generation of his comprehensive authority in all fields of knowledge [cite: 1]. The intellectual worldview of R. Chouraqui rested on the premise that education in the sciences and in worldly wisdom is not merely permitted but an obligation, required for coping intelligently with the challenges of practical life, for developing logical thinking and for establishing the moral and value-based conduct of the individual within the community [cite: 1]. In his tradition of study he took care to combine the traditions of the Sages with original inquiries, as expressed, for example, in his homilies on figures from rabbinic literature, such as his study of Rabbi Akiva, son of converts, and his homily on converts in the mystery of the crowns of the Torah [cite: 6].
Mathematical Thought and Hebrew Pedagogy: The Work "Moneh Mispar"
One of the most distinct expressions of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui's scientific and Torah teaching is his work "Moneh Mispar" (Counter of Number), which he completed in 1691 [cite: 1, 5, 7]. This book is a comprehensive treatise and textbook of arithmetic and mathematics, considered one of the first and most important works of this genre written in the Hebrew language in North Africa in the early modern period [cite: 1, 8, 9]. The work was written out of a distinctly pedagogical and public motive, its aim being to give Torah students, merchants and educated people in the communities of the Maghreb a fundamental mastery of arithmetical operations, fractions, proportions, basic algebra and the practical calculations required for commercial and calendrical needs [cite: 1, 8, 9].
The book "Moneh Mispar" was preserved for generations as a rare manuscript in the library of Jews' College in London, until it was prepared and published in a comprehensive annotated scholarly edition by the Hebrew linguist and historian of science Prof. Gad Ben-Ami Sarfatti in 1973, published by Bar-Ilan University [cite: 1, 8, 9]. The work is first-rate historical evidence of a vibrant intellectual life and of a legacy of rabbinic humanism in North Africa, in which there was no barrier between sacred wisdom and the natural sciences [cite: 8, 9]. In his linguistic and pedagogical analysis, Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui coined an original Hebrew mathematical terminology, anchoring the scientific concepts in biblical and rabbinic texts, and thereby continued the scientific tradition of the sages of Spain such as Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra and Maimonides (Rambam) [cite: 1, 8, 9].
Hermeneutical and Philosophical Exegesis: "Shir Chadash" on Psalm 119
Alongside his engagement with the exact sciences, Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui composed a wide-ranging hermeneutical exegetical work entitled "Shir Chadash" (A New Song), which was completed before his death (around the years 1704–1706) and printed in a modern edition in Jerusalem in 5760 (2000) by the Bnei Yissachar Institute [cite: 1, 10]. The work is devoted entirely to an in-depth interpretation of Psalm 119 in the Book of Psalms, the longest psalm in the Bible, which is built as an eightfold alphabetical acrostic and deals with the excellence of the Torah, the statutes and the ordinances [cite: 1, 10].
In the work "Shir Chadash," R. Chouraqui applies a multi-layered exegetical approach that blends Hebrew grammar and linguistics, philosophical inquiries, observations in the natural sciences and manifestations of the secrets of Kabbalah [cite: 1]. The work has been the subject of extensive academic research, foremost among it the doctoral dissertation of the scholar Marie Nagar at New York University, written in 1996, which saw the book as a panoramic window onto the intellectual history of the Jews of the Maghreb [cite: 1, 4]. Further studies, among them those of Prof. Yosef Charvit, have pointed out the work's contribution to understanding the thought of the sages of Algeria [cite: 1, 4]. In his interpretation, R. Chouraqui shows how the verses of the psalm reflect the cosmic order, divine providence and free will, presenting the Torah as a comprehensive system that unites spiritual law with the physical laws of nature [cite: 1].
Liturgical Poetry, the Longing for Zion and the Sabbatean Polemic
Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui was also known in the communities of Algeria and the Maghreb as an inspired poet and liturgical poet, whose poems were incorporated into the prayer books and the poetic tradition of the Jews of Algiers, Oran, Tlemcen and other communities [cite: 1, 10]. His liturgical poetry is characterized by pure biblical language and mastery of the Spanish metrical structures, and it focuses mainly on the themes of the future redemption, the longing for the Land of Israel and the yearning for the return to Zion [cite: 1, 4].
Rabbi Saadia's poetic work took on exceptional historical and religious significance against the background of the Sabbatean crisis that struck the Jewish world in the second half of the 17th century [cite: 1]. In the face of the surge of the false messianic awakening of Shabbetai Tzvi and its aftermath, R. Chouraqui mobilized his poetic and homiletical power to set up a firm barrier of faith [cite: 1]. In his poetry and his exegesis he stressed that the true redemption had not yet come, and described it as a tangible historical and national process of the ingathering of the exiles, the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the restoration of sovereignty, while utterly rejecting the Sabbatean claims regarding the abolition of the commandments or a change in the halakhic order of the world [cite: 1]. The detailed descriptions of redemption in his poems were intended to strengthen the spirit of the community, to warn against false messiahs and to ensure halakhic continuity, and several of his poems became an inseparable part of the local prayer rite in Algeria [cite: 1, 10].
The Chouraqui Family Lineage: Continuity of Spiritual, Legal and Public Leadership
The Chouraqui family represents an urban and rabbinic elite lineage whose origins lie among the exiles from Spain, which preserved its spiritual and cultural standing in North Africa for hundreds of years and from there spread to France and to the State of Israel [cite: 1, 4]. The ability to combine scrupulous loyalty to the tradition of the generations with deep involvement in law, literature and public life has remained a central characteristic of the family through the generations [cite: 1, 4, 9].
In the modern era and in the 20th century, several members of the family stood out who continued this legacy in diverse fields:
Sidney Saadia Chouraqui served as a jurist, judge and leading public figure in Algeria and in France [cite: 4, 5, 11]. During the Second World War he was vigorously active in the ranks of the Resistance – the French underground against the Nazi occupation and the Vichy regime in central France between 1942 and 1945 [cite: 4, 5]. After the war he served as a lawyer and as a judge at the Court of Appeal in Algiers, and between 1947 and 1953 he served as deputy executive secretary of the Alliance Israélite Universelle (AIU) [cite: 4, 5]. He also served as vice-president of the NGO Committee of UNICEF in the years 1950–1956, and was a prominent spokesman of Jewish and French culture [cite: 4, 5].
André Chouraqui (1917–2007) was one of the greatest thinkers, writers and jurists of the Jewish world in the 20th century [cite: 9, 12]. He grew up in Algeria, was active in France and in Israel, and served as deputy mayor of Jerusalem [cite: 9, 12]. André Chouraqui gained worldwide renown for his monumental translation project, in the framework of which he retranslated into French the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament and the Quran, preserving the linguistic emphases and the original Semitic roots [cite: 12]. The transition of the Chouraqui family from Torah and scientific leadership in Tlemcen in the 17th century to legal, cultural and diplomatic leadership in the 20th century reflects the development of Maghrebi Jewry in the modern era [cite: 1, 4, 9].
A Concise Comparison of the Books and Work of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui
Field of creativity and activity | Title of the work / creation | Dates and printed editions | Main contents and unique features
Arithmetic and mathematics | "Moneh Mispar" | Written: ~1691; printed: 1973 (Bar-Ilan University) | A Hebrew textbook of mathematics and arithmetic. Includes the development of original Hebrew terms and applied algebra [cite: 1, 5, 8, 9].
Biblical exegesis and philosophy | "Shir Chadash" | Written: ~1706; printed: 2000 (Bnei Yissachar Institute) | A comprehensive commentary on Psalm 119. Blends linguistics, natural sciences, philosophy and Kabbalah [cite: 1, 10].
Poetry and liturgical verse | Liturgical poems in the Algerian prayer books | The 17th and 18th centuries | Liturgical poems on the themes of redemption and the Land of Israel. Served as a central ideological weapon for repelling the Sabbatean movement [cite: 1, 10].
Spiritual and educational leadership | The center of learning in Tlemcen | 1603–1704 | Teaching of Torah and sciences, establishing the standing of Tlemcen as a center of Torah and knowledge in the Maghreb [cite: 1, 2, 5].
Continuity of the family legacy | Activity of members of the Chouraqui family | The 20th and 21st centuries | Continuity of legal, literary and public leadership (Sidney Saadia Chouraqui, André Chouraqui) [cite: 4, 5, 9, 12].
Summary and Research Conclusions
A comprehensive analysis of the life, writings and legacy of Rabbi Saadia Chouraqui shows that his figure constitutes a historical and ideological bridge between the tradition of the sages of Spain and the spiritual creativity of Maghrebi Jewry in the early modern period [cite: 1]. His scientific contribution in his book "Moneh Mispar" proves that the sages of Algeria in the 17th century cultivated a rabbinic-humanist worldview that saw the exact sciences as an inseparable part of Torah and religious thought [cite: 1, 8, 9]. This conception enabled R. Chouraqui to develop an original Hebrew mathematical terminology and to make practical knowledge accessible to the community, abolishing the artificial separation between sacred wisdom and secular wisdom [cite: 1, 8].
At the same time, his exegetical work in "Shir Chadash" and his liturgical poetry attest to the depth of his intellectual and religious response to the challenges of the period, foremost among them the Sabbatean crisis [cite: 1]. His response to Sabbateanism was not confined to bans of excommunication alone, but was expressed in shaping a measured and tangible messianic consciousness through the poetry of redemption and liturgical verse, while strengthening the community's loyalty to halakha and to the historical commitment to the building of Zion [cite: 1]. The remarkable continuity of the Chouraqui family through the generations – from the Torah and scientific leadership of Rabbi Saadia in Tlemcen to the legal, literary and political activity of members of the family in the 20th century – testifies to the strength of this tradition and to its lasting contribution to the Jewish people and to human culture [cite: 1, 4, 9].
